If the data is not a lab, purge the PNGs from history (git filter-repo) and force-push, accepting that forks and clones keep copies. Add a short sanitisation checklist for future doc images.

title: 19 emitted finding IDs and ~29 emitted edge types are undocumented; reference links land on sections that never mention them; ELB has no anchor
explanation:
policy_parser.py emits 69 distinct finding IDs. attack_paths.md mentions 50 of them, counting the shorthand 'PRIVESC-003/004/005', '006/007/008' and '010/011', and it names no ID that the code lacks. The 19 undocumented IDs are exactly as claimed: DANGER-001/003/004/005/006/007/009/010, PRIVESC-002/012, TRUST-002, EC2-INET-001, EC2-PROFILE-001, K8S-DEFAULT-SA, K8S-HOSTPID-001, K8S-NET-001/002, K8S-RBAC-002 and LAMBDA-XACCT-001. attack_paths.md:308 says 'These are the 20 detection rules', but the table (:310-324) covers 18 and omits PRIVESC-002 and PRIVESC-012.
_doc_reference (policy_parser.py:3784-3789) still attaches a section URL to each of these IDs, and that section never mentions the ID. _DOC_ANCHORS (policy_parser.py:3761-3781) has no 'ELB' key, so ELB-PUB-001 links to the bare document. ELB-PUB-001 is listed in Scenario 6 (:259) but not in the Resource-Exposure table.
The edge reference table (:372-410) omits about 29 emitted types. Examples are CAN_READ_SECRET, CAN_WRITE_SECRET, CAN_READ_PARAM, SECRET_/PARAM_ENCRYPTED_BY, SECRET_GRANTS_*, LAMBDA_GRANTS_*, ECR_/DDB_GRANTS_*, KMS_GRANT, CAN_ENCRYPT, CAN_MODIFY_CONFIG, CAN_ADMIN_MSG, CAN_ADMIN_SG, GRANTS_ACCESS, HAS_SG, SG_ALLOWS_FROM and CLUSTER_ROLE. MEMBER_OF, HAS_POLICY, CAN_MANAGE and IN_CLUSTER appear only in prose.
I re-rated this to low. Every finding JSON already carries title, description and remediation, and most edge names explain themselves, so operators are not left without information. Only the promised doc cross-reference is broken. Field data shows the gap is frequent rather than marginal: undocumented IDs make up 40-55% of findings in recent local runs.
evidence:
Regex diff (scratchpad agents/docs/code_ids.txt vs doc_ids_exp.txt): 69 code IDs, 50 documented, 19 undocumented, 0 doc-only.
_doc_reference outputs: ELB-PUB-001 -> (no anchor); TRUST-002 -> #scenario-6-... (that section mentions only TRUST-001); DANGER-005 -> #high-value-targets-to-hunt (mentions only DANGER-002); EC2-INET-001 -> #scenario-1-... (mentions only EC2-IMDS-001 by ID).
Anonymised field counts from the 3 most recent local runs: undocumented findings 80/146, 59/130, 53/123. TRUST-002 has 13/18/17 occurrences and is the top or second ID in each run. CAN_READ_PARAM is the most numerous edge in the latest run (337).
impact: The 📖 'attack path' link for nearly half of real-world findings opens a section that says nothing about them, including the very common TRUST-002 and DANGER-001. The field guide gives no guidance for the secret/parameter edges that dominate real graphs. This is a usability and trust cost, not a graph-accuracy error.
fix: Add rows for the 19 IDs. Put DANGER-* in a 'Dangerous permissions' table with its own anchor, add PRIVESC-002 and PRIVESC-012 to the privesc table, add TRUST-002 to a cross-account trust section, and add the K8s and EC2 extras to their scenarios. Add 'ELB' to _DOC_ANCHORS and an ELB-PUB-001 row. Extend the edge table with the missing types. Add a unit test that parses policy_parser for finding IDs and edge types and asserts each one appears in attack_paths.md, and that every _DOC_ANCHORS anchor resolves to a heading.

title: README 'Run directly' installs only boto3; without kubernetes, K8s/IRSA enumeration fails (with a warning, not silently)
explanation:
The omission is real. readme.md:94 says `pip install boto3`, while requirements.txt and pyproject both declare kubernetes. eks_auth.build_k8s_client imports kubernetes lazily at line 64, before it requests a token. k8s._enumerate_cluster catches the ModuleNotFoundError at k8s.py:61-68 and records auth_status 'failed', so pods, service accounts and RBAC are never collected and the IRSA_BRIDGE edges and K8s findings disappear.
The 'silently / no clear message' part is wrong. k8s.enumerate prints a per-cluster warning that names the missing module (k8s.py:228) and a summary line '0/N clusters accessible' (k8s.py:232). cluster_info.json also records the error.
Only the 'no install' path is affected. pipx, pip install -e (pyproject dependencies) and Docker (Dockerfile: pip install -r requirements.txt) all install kubernetes. The repo's local .venv does lack kubernetes, but that is the developer's environment, not a shipped artefact.
evidence:
Synthetic run (no AWS: MagicMock session, a fake eks/clusters.json with one cluster) using the repo .venv, which has no kubernetes:
  [+] K8s Enumeration Starting...
  [!] Cluster c1: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'kubernetes'
  [+] K8s Enumeration Finished (0/1 clusters accessible)
  cluster_info.json: {"auth_status": "failed", "error": "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'kubernetes'"}
`.venv/bin/python -c 'import kubernetes'` gives ModuleNotFoundError.
impact: An operator who follows the 'Run directly' instructions loses all Kubernetes RBAC and IRSA attack paths, which the README calls the 'killer edge'. The console shows a module-not-found warning per cluster, so the gap is visible to an attentive operator but easy to misread as an EKS access-entry or auth problem.
fix: Change readme.md:94 to `pip install -r requirements.txt`. In k8s.enumerate, check importlib.util.find_spec('kubernetes') once before looping. If it is missing, print a single clear hint ('pip install kubernetes to enable K8s/IRSA enumeration') and write auth_status 'dependency_missing' rather than 'failed'.

title: Dead code (no-op target_id, unused known_arns/igw_vpcs/account_id parameter, redundant `== '*'` checks) and no unit tests for the analysis engine
explanation: All the cited items exist. `target_id = pval if pval in known_arns else pval` (:1046) returns pval either way, and known_arns (:969-975) is used nowhere else; the same unused set is built again at :1739-1745. igw_vpcs (:1321-1324) is filled and never read. _analyze_trust_policies(roles, account_id=None) (:714) never uses account_id, and analyze() calls it without one (:3829). In `_action_matches(action, 's3:*') or action == '*'` (:869, similarly :1199, :1648, :1670, :2033, :2329), the second check is redundant because fnmatch('s3:*', '*') is already true. git ls-files shows no test files, conftest or pytest config in the 89 tracked files. None of this changes output today. The missing tests are why regressions like the single-object Statement crash went unnoticed.
evidence: grep: known_arns appears only at :969-975, :1046 and :1739-1745. igw_vpcs appears only at :1321 and :1324. `git ls-files | grep -i test` returns nothing.
impact: No user-facing effect. The no-op at :1046 suggests principal-to-node resolution was intended but never implemented. With no tests, the roughly 4,000-line detection engine can regress silently.
fix: Delete the no-op lines and unused sets, or implement the intended known-entity resolution. Remove the unused account_id parameter, or use it for the trust analysis fallback. Drop the redundant `or action == '*'` checks. Add a pytest suite that builds synthetic report directories, as in this verification (trust single-object, federated, wildcard plus condition, BPA/ACL, ARN wildcards, dedup), and run it in CI.

title: Legacy S3 LocationConstraint 'EU' stored verbatim as bucket Region
explanation: s3.py:60 stores LocationConstraint or 'us-east-1', so legacy eu-west-1 buckets that return 'EU' are recorded as Region 'EU'. The claimed impact on region-based joins is wrong: the parser never reads bucket Region (policy_parser.py:902-906 uses only Name), and the dashboard only displays it (index.html:2454 `field('Region', d.entityData.Region)`). The effect is cosmetic.
evidence: s3.py:60 `bucket_info["Region"] = loc.get("LocationConstraint") or "us-east-1"`. Stub with LocationConstraint 'EU' gives buckets.json Region "EU". grep finds no Region consumer in policy_parser.py and only the one display line in index.html.
impact: A legacy bucket's displayed region reads 'EU' instead of 'eu-west-1'. No effect on findings or graph edges.
fix: Normalize: `region = loc.get('LocationConstraint') or 'us-east-1'; region = {'EU': 'eu-west-1'}.get(region, region)`.

title: Dashboard server enables directory listing and accepts any Host header (static public assets only)
explanation: The stock SimpleHTTPRequestHandler is used (dashboard.py:40). It auto-lists directories and does not validate Host, so DNS rebinding is possible. The server binds 127.0.0.1 only, and it serves just app/dashboard (index.html plus SVG icons). Reports are loaded client-side from a user-chosen zip and are never served, so a rebinding page could read only public static files. Traversal is blocked.
evidence:
dashboard.py:40 `functools.partial(http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler, directory=directory)`.
Repro (dash.py): GET /icons/ -> 200 with 'Directory listing'; GET / with Host: evil.example -> 200; GET /../utils/dashboard.py -> 404; GET /%2e%2e/main.py -> 404.
impact: Negligible today. It would matter only if the server later served report data (for example a 'load from reports/' feature).
fix: Subclass the handler: override list_directory to return 404, and reject requests whose Host is not 127.0.0.1:<port> or localhost:<port>. Keep this hardening in place before ever serving report files.

title: regions.json is shipped as package data but never read
explanation: pyproject.toml:39 packages app/utils/regions.json. No Python, HTML or other code in app/ references it; the only other mention is the README tree (readme.md:217). It is dead data, and it is the natural fallback for the unguarded DescribeRegions call.
evidence: `grep -rn 'regions.json' app pyproject.toml readme.md docs` returns only pyproject.toml:39 and readme.md:217.
impact: No functional impact. It is a missed opportunity to make --all resilient when DescribeRegions is denied.
fix: Use it as the fallback in get_enabled_regions (filtered by partition), or remove it from package-data and the README.

title: No BloodHound OpenGraph / graph-DB export; graph only exists inside the bespoke dashboard
explanation:
This is a feature gap, not a defect. readme.md:3 positions the tool as 'inspired by BloodHound'. A grep of app/ and pyproject finds no OpenGraph, Cypher, Neo4j, GraphML or GEXF output. analyze() writes only bespoke analysis/*.json (policy_parser.py:3887-3928).
An exporter is harder than it looks because the graph is not fully built in Python. Several nodes and edges are assembled only in the browser: MEMBER_OF, HAS_POLICY, CAN_ASSUME/CAN_ASSUME_CROSS, the dashboard's INSTANCE_ROLE and SSRF_TO_IMDS (index.html:1163-1249), plus placeholder external principals. An exporter would first need to move that assembly into Python.
The ecosystem claims cannot be checked from the repo. BloodHound CE v8 introduced OpenGraph in mid-2025, which matches my knowledge. The 'AWSHound (2026-08)' claim is later than what I can confirm.
evidence: `grep -rniE 'opengraph|cypher|neo4j|bloodhound|graphml|gexf' app/ pyproject.toml` returns no matches. Edge construction with makeEdge(...) happens only in index.html:1170-1247.
impact: Users cannot merge aws-enumerator's distinctive K8s RBAC/IRSA and resource-exposure edges with other graph sources, or run ad-hoc Cypher queries. Analysis is limited to the single-file dashboard's Dijkstra and visual inspection.
fix: Move graph assembly (nodes plus every edge source, including the dashboard-built IAM, trust and instance edges) into a Python build_graph() that writes analysis/graph.json. Then add `--export opengraph` that maps node types and edge kinds to the OpenGraph JSON schema, and have the dashboard consume graph.json so both outputs stay consistent.

title: Python 3.10 fnmatch compiled-pattern cache (256 entries) thrashes for entities with >256 distinct actions, causing a ~10-25x analysis slowdown
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed and reproduced locally with no AWS calls. _action_matches (policy_parser.py:346-348) calls fnmatch.fnmatch(action.lower(), pattern.lower()), and _entity_has_action (:351-358) uses each of the entity's actions as the pattern. On CPython 3.10.11 (the repo .venv) fnmatch._compile_pattern is lru_cache(maxsize=256). On 3.11.14, 3.12.13, 3.13.14 and 3.14.6 it is maxsize=32768 (checked in the installed stdlib sources). requires-python is >=3.10 (pyproject.toml:11). With more than 256 distinct action strings in one entity, each rule check cycles the cache and recompiles regexes. That is common: SecurityAudit alone has ~1,199 actions, and ReadOnlyAccess has a similar number. My benchmark of the real _detect_privesc_paths on one role: 3.10 gives 17 ms (250 actions), 38 ms (260), 263 ms (600), 1,115 ms (1,500); 3.13 gives 10, 3.5, 16.5 and 44 ms. That is a cliff of about 25x at 1,500 actions. The same matcher feeds the dangerous-permission and resource analyzers, so F-030's slowness compounds on 3.10. Results are unaffected, the Docker image uses 3.13 and the problem is version-specific, so it is rated low rather than medium. It is a distinct root cause from F-030 (missing service prefilter) and is linked to it.
evidence: .venv/bin/python -c 'fnmatch._compile_pattern.cache_info()' -> maxsize=256; inspect.getsource(fnmatch) on 3.11-3.14 -> lru_cache(maxsize=32768). Benchmark scratchpad/agents/verify-new-1/fnbench.py: 3.10.11 [250: 17.2 ms, 260: 38.4 ms, 600: 263.3 ms, 1500: 1114.5 ms]; 3.13.14 [10.0, 3.5, 16.5, 43.8 ms]; 0 findings in each case, so results are identical.
impact: On Python 3.10 hosts (the project's own venv, Ubuntu 22.04's system Python, pipx installs on it), accounts with many ReadOnly/SecurityAudit-style roles take minutes longer to analyse, multiplying F-030.
fix: Replace fnmatch in the hot path with `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None) def _glob_re(p): return re.compile(fnmatch.translate(p.lower()))` and `_glob_re(pattern).match(action.lower())`, and lower-case the action sets once when the permission map is built. Alternatively raise requires-python to >=3.11. Add a micro-benchmark test.

title: Findings have no stable fingerprint, run context, baseline/diff or suppression, and their natural key (id, entity_arn) collides
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Merged: both describe one missing contract, that a finding has no stable identity or provenance. Confirmed. Privesc findings are dicts of id/severity/category/title/entity/entity_arn/description/matched_actions/source_policy/source_type/resource/remediation (policy_parser.py:579-596), and other analyzers use the same shape. There is no fingerprint, confidence or first_seen field. findings.json is written as a bare {'findings': [...]} (:3887-3888) with no account, region, run timestamp or version. That context exists only in the sibling manifest.json. (id, entity_arn) is not unique. EC2-EXPOSURE-001 is appended inside the per-SG loop with entity_arn=inst_id and resource=[inst_id], so an instance with two open SGs yields two findings that differ only in source_policy, title and ports (:1462-1497). EBS-XACCT-001 is appended once per SharedAccounts entry with the same entity_arn (:3131-3138). grep finds no baseline, diff or suppression support in app/. This is a feature gap, not an accuracy defect, so it is rated low rather than medium. It is not covered by the register: F-018/F-086 are about finding noise and F-141 about graph export. Cross-file: relates to P3-021 (manifest integrity) and P3-028 (naive timestamps).
evidence: policy_parser.py:579-596 finding dict; :3884-3888 json.dump({'findings': findings}); :1462-1497 EC2-EXPOSURE-001 inside `for sg_ref in inst.get('SecurityGroups')`; :3131-3138 EBS-XACCT-001 per `acct in snap.get('SharedAccounts')`; grep -riE 'baseline|suppress|fingerprint' app/ -> no feature code.
impact: Repeat assessments of the same account cannot show new, fixed or accepted findings. Findings exported to a SIEM or ticketing system lose account and run provenance. Exporters must invent composite keys, and keys built on source_policy change when policies are renamed.
fix: Add a deterministic `fingerprint` (sha256 of id, account, entity_arn, sorted resource and a rule-specific discriminator such as sg_id or target account) to every finding. Wrap findings.json as {schema_version, tool_version, account_id, regions, generated_at (UTC), findings}. Add `--baseline <old findings.json>` to emit new/resolved/unchanged, and `--suppress <file>` (fingerprint plus reason plus expiry) that marks findings as suppressed rather than dropping them.

title: Product name collides with an older public tool, PyPI name is unclaimed (squatting risk), and UI is branded with the personal handle
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. index.html:6 has `<title>0xj4f AWS Attack Graph</title>`. The CLI banner shows 'Author: 0xj4f' (app/main.py:34). The manifest hard-codes "author": "0xj4f" (main.py:70). pyproject.toml:6 names the distribution aws-enumerator, but https://pypi.org/pypi/aws-enumerator/json returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-12, so the name is unclaimed. A separate public Go project, shabarkin/aws-enumerator (created 2021-04-11, about 272 stars), exists, as confirmed by a read-only GitHub API lookup. The branding and discoverability points are product opinions. The one concrete risk is that an unclaimed PyPI name for a tool that runs with AWS credentials can be squatted: users who type `pipx install aws-enumerator` instead of the README's git URL would install whatever a squatter publishes. Low.
evidence: index.html:6; app/main.py:34 banner, :70 manifest author; pyproject.toml:6 name; curl https://pypi.org/pypi/aws-enumerator/json -> 404; gh api repos/shabarkin/aws-enumerator -> Go, created 2021-04-11.
impact: Confusion with the older tool in search results and reports. A squatted PyPI package could deliver malicious code to users holding AWS credentials.
fix: Register the PyPI name (or a distinct product name) with trusted publishing, even as a placeholder that points to the repo. Consider a distinct product name. Brand the dashboard title and banner with the product name and keep the author in metadata only.

title: Dashboard loads only .zip reports, but zipping is opt-in, the end-of-run hint never mentions --zip, and dropping a non-zip does nothing
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The mechanics check out. The file input is accept=".zip" (index.html:598). The drop handler calls loadZipFile only when the name ends in .zip and otherwise does nothing, with no message (:906-908). There is no folder loader (no webkitdirectory or webkitGetAsEntry). --zip is opt-in (main.py:186, :251, :277). The README's first run example (readme.md:67) has no --zip, and main.py:284 always prints "run 'aws-enumerator --dashboard' and load the report", even when no zip was made. The claim is narrower than stated: readme.md:68 shows `--all --zip`, the dashboard section says to drop the .zip (:122), and both the server and the overlay say .zip (dashboard.py:56, index.html:729). Users are told what to load, so this is friction plus a silent no-op, not an impossible flow. It is not in the register; F-092 and F-094 are different load-path bugs.
evidence: index.html:598 `accept=".zip"`; index.html:906-908 `if (file && file.name.endsWith('.zip')) { await loadZipFile(file); }` with no else branch; index.html:729 and dashboard.py:56 ask for a .zip; readme.md:67 `aws-enumerator --region eu-west-2`; main.py:284 prints the dashboard hint whether or not args.zip is set.
impact: A first-time user who runs the headline command gets a report folder the dashboard cannot open, and gets no feedback when they drop it. They must zip it by hand or re-run the whole AWS crawl.
fix: When --zip was not passed, print a zip hint (or zip by default and add --no-zip). In the dashboard, show an error for non-zip drops and add a folder picker (`<input webkitdirectory>` / DataTransferItem.webkitGetAsEntry) that fills the same files map processLoadedFiles already takes.

title: Dashboard never uses the manifest caller_arn to find the operator's own principal, and assumed-role/SSO STS ARNs are not mapped to IAM role nodes
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. reportData.manifest is assigned at index.html:1016 and never read; grep finds no other manifest, run_metadata, caller or assumed-role reference in the dashboard. policy_parser.py has no caller handling either. main.py:76 writes caller_arn. A repro of main() with stubbed STS wrote the raw `arn:aws:sts::<acct>:assumed-role/<RoleName>/<session>` form. That form drops the role path, so it never equals an IAM role node ID. This is related to F-043 (the owned set is ignored by Discover All Paths) but distinct: even after F-043 is fixed, the operator still has to find and mark their own node by hand. Mapping by role name within the same account is safe because role names are unique per account.
evidence: grep -n 'manifest|caller|assumed-role' app/dashboard/index.html -> :943-952 (root detection) and :1016 `reportData.manifest = readJSON('manifest.json') || {};` only; app/main.py:76 `"caller_arn": caller_identity['Arn']`; no 'caller' in app/components/*.py.
impact: Every assumed-breach run starts with the operator searching the graph for their own identity before asking what it can reach. Combined with F-043, the tool never answers 'what can I reach?' by default.
fix: On load, read manifest.run_metadata.caller_arn. For an iam user ARN, use it as the node ID directly. For an sts assumed-role ARN, find the role node whose RoleName is the second path segment in the same account. Highlight that node, add it to window._ownedNodes, and make it the default Find Path source (with F-043's fix, Discover All Paths then starts from it). Show 'caller not in graph' when nothing matches, for example for a cross-account or federated session.

title: API Gateway per-method GetIntegration and Lambda per-function GetFunctionUrlConfig/GetPolicy loops consume fixed, shared account control-plane quotas (production throttling risk)
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The code facts hold. apigateway.py:38-48 issues one get_integration per method on top of GetResources pages, plus get_authorizers per API (:54). Throttle-exhausted integrations are dropped by `except ClientError: continue` (:47-48). lambda_.py:68-76 calls get_function_url_config for every function, then :89-96 calls get_policy for every function, both sequentially. The cited quotas are consistent with AWS documentation as I know it: API Gateway total management operations about 10 rps with burst 40, Lambda GetPolicy 15 rps, and the 'remainder of control plane' bucket 15 rps, all not adjustable. I did not fetch the quota pages. F-100 already records the API Gateway fan-out, the ~10 rps account quota and the silent drop, but frames it as runtime and noise. The new angle is the shared-tenant effect. With adaptive retry (main.py:202-203) the scanner's client converges on whatever rate the bucket allows, so during a scan it can take most of the account's API Gateway or Lambda control-plane budget, and concurrent deployments (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform) see TooManyRequestsException. The Lambda loops are also not in F-100. Severity lowered to low: the effect lasts only while those modules run, IaC tools retry throttles, and the F-100 fix (GetResources embed=methods) removes most of the API Gateway calls. The '91% of budget' figure is simple arithmetic (sequential calls at 100 ms ≈ 9-10 rps), not a measurement. Cross-file overlap: P3-025 (no client-side request budget).
evidence: apigateway.py:38-48 per-method get_integration loop, :47-48 silent continue, :54 get_authorizers; lambda_.py:68-76 get_function_url_config per function, :89-96 get_policy per function; main.py:202-203 AWS_RETRY_MODE=adaptive, AWS_MAX_ATTEMPTS=10.
impact: Scans of production accounts with large REST APIs or many functions can briefly throttle the owner's deployments and control-plane automation in that region. Under sustained throttling the scanner silently loses Lambda targets.
fix: Apply F-100 (paginate get_resources with embed=['methods'] and PageSize 500, and read methodIntegration inline). Add a client-side token bucket per service, for example ≤3 rps for apigateway and ≤5 rps for Lambda GetPolicy and control-plane calls, exposed through a --max-rps or --polite flag. Skip get_function_url_config when ListFunctionUrlConfigs or the function's config indicates no URL, or make it opt-in. Record throttled-and-dropped items instead of `continue`.

title: IAM credential hygiene (root MFA/keys, console users without MFA, active key age, password policy) is collected but never evaluated
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. _enumerate_account_level (iam.py:53-75) writes account_password_policy.json and account_summary.json (SummaryMap includes AccountMFAEnabled and AccountAccessKeysPresent). Per-user data includes AccessKeys, MFADevices and HasLoginProfile. A case-insensitive grep of policy_parser.py for mfa|access_key|password_policy|account_summary|login_profile matches only the PRIVESC-009/010/011 rule names and remediation strings (:73-86), with no evaluation of the collected data. Neither account file is read anywhere else in app/. The dashboard only displays per-user MFA, console and active-key values (index.html:1074-1076, :2423-2427) and raises no finding. readme.md:14 advertises collection of 'access keys, MFA, console access ... account password policy'. This is the same 'collected but not analysed' pattern as F-046, which covers the logging and network data, so it is linked as related. It is new for identity hygiene, and console users without MFA plus root keys are directly relevant to initial access. The CIS/FSBP mapping is the reporter's framing and was not checked control by control.
evidence: iam.py:53-75, :97-135; grep -niE 'mfa|access_?key|password_policy|account_summary|login_?profile' app/components/policy_parser.py -> only lines 73-86 (rule definitions); grep account_password_policy|account_summary in app/ -> iam.py only; index.html:1074-1076, :2423-2427 display only.
impact: Root access keys, a root account without MFA, console users without MFA, and stale active keys go unreported even though the data is in the bundle. These are among the most common real initial-access paths.
fix: Add an _analyze_identity_hygiene pass that emits IAM-ROOT-MFA-001 (AccountMFAEnabled == 0), IAM-ROOT-KEY-001 (AccountAccessKeysPresent > 0), IAM-USER-MFA-001 (HasLoginProfile and no MFADevices), IAM-KEY-AGE-001 (an Active key older than 90 days), and IAM-PWPOL-001 (no policy, or a weak one). Optionally use GenerateCredentialReport for last-used data (see F-109/F-110).

title: Kubernetes collector issues unpaginated cluster-wide LISTs (pods, secrets, etc.) with no limit/continue
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed: every list call in k8s.py (:97, :104, :111, :118, :125, :132, :139, :146, :163, :170) is made without limit or _continue, and a grep for limit=|_continue|_request_timeout|resource_version in k8s.py and eks_auth.py finds nothing. Unlike AWS APIs, an unbounded Kubernetes LIST is not truncated. The apiserver builds the whole list in one response and the client deserialises every object, so on large clusters this costs apiserver/etcd work and scanner memory. The parts that are already registered: the missing request timeout is F-120; full Secret payloads being pulled into memory, and the metadata-only Accept fix, are F-009/F-062. The Helm-secret size impact is the reporter's estimate (not measured), and API Priority and Fairness limits the damage to the apiserver. What remains new is pagination, which is the Kubernetes counterpart of F-107's unpaginated AWS list calls. Severity stays low.
evidence: k8s.py:104 core_v1.list_pod_for_all_namespaces(); :146 core_v1.list_secret_for_all_namespaces(); grep -cE 'limit=|_continue|_request_timeout|resource_version' app/components/k8s.py app/utils/eks_auth.py -> 0 and 0.
impact: On very large clusters a scan causes apiserver and etcd load spikes, and scanner memory grows with the size of the cluster's objects. Secret LISTs in Helm-heavy clusters can be especially large.
fix: Add a helper that pages with limit=500 and _continue for every list_*_for_all_namespaces call, and pass _request_timeout=(5, 60) (F-120). For secrets, see P3-007: drop the call or make it opt-in. If it is kept, use the PartialObjectMetadataList Accept header.

title: K8s secret listing requires cluster-wide 'list secrets' RBAC for data no analyzer consumes; the register's metadata-only fix does not reduce the grant
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Mostly correct. _list_secrets calls core_v1.list_secret_for_all_namespaces() (k8s.py:145-157), which needs the RBAC verb 'list' on secrets cluster-wide. In Kubernetes, 'list' on secrets lets the holder read full Secret objects, data included, regardless of the Accept header the client sends. So the metadata-only (PartialObjectMetadataList) fix recommended in F-009/F-062 stops values being transferred but does not shrink the privilege an operator must grant. secrets.json is loaded (policy_parser.py:3253-3257) but never consumed: the only k8ssecret nodes come from pod volume references (the secret_vol/secret_name block in _analyze_k8s_relationships), and the dashboard does not read secrets.json. Removing the listing therefore loses no analysis. Overstated: 'forces' a grant. The call is wrapped in _safe_call (k8s.py:157), so a 403 is recorded and the rest of the cluster enumeration continues. The pressure to grant comes from wanting an error-free run and from the lack of any documented K8s RBAC (cross-file P3-033). F-009 already notes that nothing downstream needs secrets.json, and F-062 covers the missing K8s opt-out. What is new is the observation that the proposed fix does not achieve least privilege, so the fix for F-009/F-062 should change. Rated low: the overall K8s-scope risk is already rated medium in F-062.
evidence: k8s.py:144-157 _list_secrets / _safe_call('secrets', ...); policy_parser.py:3253-3257 loads 'secrets' into cluster_data; grep shows k8ssecret node creation only from pod volume 'secret_name'; index.html has no secrets.json read; F-009/F-062 fix text recommends the metadata-only Accept header.
impact: Operators who give the scanner a ClusterRole that matches its calls hand it a 'read every Secret in every cluster' credential for no analytic benefit, and the planned remediation would leave that grant in place.
fix: Remove the cluster-wide secret listing, or put it behind an explicit --k8s-secrets opt-in. Derive k8ssecret nodes only from pod volume, envFrom and env references. Publish a minimal read-only ClusterRole with no 'secrets' rule. Amend the F-009/F-062 fix to prefer removal over the Accept header.

title: No published permission set; AWS SecurityAudit (v94) lacks wafv2:GetRuleGroup, wafv2:GetIPSet, eks:ListAddons and eks:DescribeAddon used by collectors
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The core claim is confirmed independently. I fetched the AWS managed-policy reference page for SecurityAudit (v94, edited 2026-09-30); its action set is identical to the analyst's copy. It lists wafv2 Get/List actions but not wafv2:GetRuleGroup or wafv2:GetIPSet, and eks actions but not eks:ListAddons or eks:DescribeAddon. There are no wafv2:* or eks:* wildcards. Those calls are at waf.py:95, waf.py:118, eks.py:98 and eks.py:103. My own crude sweep of collector calls against the policy found no other true gaps once naming differences are allowed for: apigateway is covered by the resource-scoped apigateway:GET statement, s3:GetBucket* covers PublicAccessBlock, and ListBuckets maps to s3:ListAllMyBuckets. No documented required-permissions policy exists in the repo. Overstated: 'silently'. Failures are written into the output as {'Error': ...} entries (waf.py:101-105, eks.py:107-110), but nothing is printed and there is no run-level status (F-061). The practical analysis impact today is nil: no analyzer or dashboard view reads WAF rule groups, IP sets or EKS add-ons (F-046). Rated low for the missing permission documentation. Cross-file: overlaps P3-027 and P3-033 (no documented permissions policy).
evidence: SecurityAudit v94 (docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/SecurityAudit.html) wafv2 entries: GetLoggingConfiguration, GetWebACL, GetWebACLForResource, ListAvailableManagedRuleGroups, ListIPSets, ListLoggingConfigurations, ListRegexPatternSets, ListResourcesForWebACL, ListRuleGroups, ListTagsForResource, ListWebACLs; eks entries: DescribeAccessEntry, DescribeCluster, DescribeFargateProfile, DescribeNodeGroup, ListAccessEntries, ListAssociatedAccessPolicies, ListClusters, ListFargateProfiles, ListNodeGroups, ListTagsForResource, ListUpdates. Code: waf.py:95 get_rule_group, :118 get_ip_set; eks.py:98 list_addons, :103 describe_addon. Script: scratchpad/agents/verify-new-1/sa_check.py.
impact: Operators running with the most common audit policy get per-item Error entries for WAF details and EKS add-ons with no console signal. Without a published policy, every new collector can widen the gap unnoticed.
fix: Publish docs/iam-policy.json: SecurityAudit plus a small supplementary statement (wafv2:GetRuleGroup, wafv2:GetIPSet, eks:ListAddons, eks:DescribeAddon), or a standalone least-privilege policy generated from the collectors. Add a CI check that diffs the collectors' boto3 calls against it. Surface per-module denied counts (F-061).

title: Kubernetes enumeration can only authenticate as the AWS caller via a presigned EKS token: no kubeconfig, SA-token or in-cluster input, and no SelfSubjectRulesReview
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. build_k8s_client (eks_auth.py:62-75) sets api_key only from get_eks_token(session), a presigned STS GetCallerIdentity URL. k8s.py:62 is the only call site. grep finds no kubeconfig, load_incluster_config, token option or SelfSubject* review. If the IAM caller is not mapped in aws-auth or an access entry, the /version probe fails, auth_status is set to 'failed' and collection stops (k8s.py:78-93). F-033 point (4) already records that the analyzer ignores auth_status, so the cluster looks empty, and F-050 covers the missing IAM-to-K8s identity mapping. A related gap: with only namespaced RBAC, the cluster-wide list calls return 403 into _safe_call error stubs (k8s.py:30-35), and there is no namespaced fallback. A SelfSubjectRulesReview would show what is listable. The new angle is alternative credential inputs and permission probing. The field-run statistics in the report were not verifiable and are not needed. Given F-062, the extra K8s-plane activity should stay opt-in.
evidence: eks_auth.py:66 `token = get_eks_token(cluster_name, session)`, :73 `config.api_key = {"authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}`; k8s.py:62 sole call; k8s.py:78-93 version probe then early return on failure; grep kubeconfig|load_incluster|SelfSubject in app/ -> none.
impact: A compromised pod's ServiceAccount token (the field guide's Scenario 2 foothold), or a kubeconfig the operator already holds, cannot be used. Clusters the AWS caller is not mapped into yield nothing, and namespaced-only access is never discovered.
fix: Add --kubeconfig/--kube-context and --k8s-endpoint/--k8s-token options plus an in-cluster mode, built with kubernetes.config.load_kube_config / load_incluster_config. Run SelfSubjectRulesReview per namespace and save the result. Fall back to namespaced lists on a cluster-wide 403. Surface auth_status in findings (F-033).

title: Single-region mode always re-collects global services (IAM, S3, CloudFront, WAF CLOUDFRONT scope, Route 53), so per-region invocations repeat the heaviest global crawl
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Both reports describe the same root cause, so they are merged. The behaviour is confirmed. A stubbed main() run with `--region eu-west-2` invoked iam, s3, cloudfront, waf (scope=None, which defaults to BOTH, waf.py:5, 19-20) and route53, at main.py:103, 107, 110, 111 and 132, and wrote all of them under reports/<date>/<acct>/<region>/. Running N regions this way repeats the per-entity IAM crawl and the 10 S3 calls per bucket (F-109) N times, multiplies the CloudTrail events, and writes N copies of iam/. Only partially a defect: single-region output is meant to be a self-contained report, because the analyzer and dashboard read iam/ from the same root, and --all exists to avoid the duplication. The cost appears when operators loop single-region runs, which they are pushed to by F-010 (regional analysis empty in --all) and the lack of a region-subset option (F-064's fix suggests --regions). No register finding tracks the duplication itself. The nearest remedy is module selection (F-062, F-125 --skip), hence the duplicate_of link. Cross-file: P3-003 in new-1 covers shared management quotas.
evidence: Repro (scratchpad agents/verify-new-2/repro_main.py, all collectors stubbed): single-region calls = [('iam', None), ('s3', None), ('cloudfront', None), ('waf', None), ('route53', None)]. main.py:101-135 enumerate_single_region; main.py:260 base_path per region; waf.py:5 `def enumerate(session, path, scope="BOTH")`.
impact: Per-region workflows multiply the slowest and noisiest part of the run (IAM N+1, S3 per-bucket, Route 53 at a low account-wide quota) by the number of regions. Report trees also grow with duplicate global data.
fix: After fixing F-010, add `--regions a,b` so a region subset uses the --all layout (global once). Add --skip-global or --global-from <path> to reuse an existing global/ tree for the same date and account instead of re-collecting it. When globals are reused, run waf with scope="REGIONAL" only.

title: No client-side request budget: adaptive retry only reacts after the first throttle, per client, so scans can consume shared account-wide control-plane quotas used by co-tenant automation
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The core mechanics are confirmed. Load control is only the setdefault of AWS_RETRY_MODE and AWS_MAX_ATTEMPTS (main.py:202-203). In botocore 1.37.34, ClientRateLimiter starts with _enabled=False, does not acquire tokens until a throttling error arrives (retries/adaptive.py:54-60, :77-88), and keeps its state per client. 'Collectors keep recreating clients' is overstated: each module creates its client once (for example s3.py:29, sg.py:9). However, five modules each create their own EC2 client per region (vpc.py:9, sg.py:9, ec2.py:9, flowlogs.py:7, ebs.py:21), so what the limiter learns is not shared. One quota figure is wrong: Route 53 allows 5 requests per second per account, not 10, which strengthens the point. Co-tenant throttling is plausible for the per-SG DescribeNetworkInterfaces loop, Route 53 listing and per-revision ECS describes (F-049). It is transient, though: other callers retry, and the tool backs off after its first throttle. The offline simulation percentages were not reproduced. The root cause, no request budget, is already F-109 (title and fix: --max-requests-per-minute). F-127 calls per-client buckets moot, and this refines that. The new angle is impact on other workloads, so this is partially-confirmed and rated low rather than medium. Cross-file: P3-003 in new-1 (API Gateway/Lambda fan-out against shared quotas) has the same root.
evidence: main.py:202-203; botocore/retries/adaptive.py:54 `self._enabled = False`, :57-59 tokens acquired only `if self._enabled`, :80-88 enabled on the first throttling response; separate session.client('ec2') in vpc.py:9, sg.py:9, ec2.py:9, flowlogs.py:7, ebs.py:21.
impact: While a scan runs on a busy production account, deploy pipelines and controllers that share the per-account Route 53, EC2 Describe, ECS and Lambda control-plane buckets can see extra throttling. Once 10 attempts are exhausted, the scanner drops items, and records them inconsistently (F-058/F-059).
fix: As in F-109: a shared client-side token bucket on before-send for every client, with --max-rps (a low default, and lower for route53). Reuse one client per service per region. Document running scans off-peak against production accounts.

title: No interrupt or SIGTERM handling and the manifest is written only after all loops, so interrupted, timed-out or OOM-killed runs leave unmarked partial trees
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. main() has no signal handler and no try/finally. run_module catches only Exception (main.py:95-98), so KeyboardInterrupt propagates. In a repro with stubbed collectors and a KeyboardInterrupt raised in lambda, main() raised KeyboardInterrupt, no manifest.json was written anywhere, and the region folder was left with 14 module directories. SIGTERM's default action kills the process without running finally blocks, and SIGKILL (OOM) cannot be caught at all. Existing coverage: F-064's fix already says to 'Generate the manifest in a finally block so partial runs are still described'; F-063 covers partial trees merging into later same-day runs; F-127 covers the lack of resume. The new angle is that a finally block alone does not cover SIGTERM (a handler is needed) or SIGKILL (a start-of-run 'in_progress' marker is needed). Completeness must therefore be recorded positively.
evidence: Repro (scratchpad agents/verify-new-2/repro_main.py): `interrupt in lambda -> KeyboardInterrupt | manifests: [] | dirs: ['cloudfront','cloudtrail','ec2','eks','flowlogs','iam','k8s','lambda','s3','secretsmanager','sg','ssm','vpc','waf']`; grep signal|SIGTERM|KeyboardInterrupt in app/ -> only utils/dashboard.py:64.
impact: A run killed by a scheduler timeout or OOM looks like a complete report folder with no manifest. A later same-day run then absorbs it into its own manifest and zip (F-063), with no indication that the data is incomplete.
fix: Write manifest.json at start with status "in_progress" and a run_id, update it per module (F-061 module_status), and set "complete" or "interrupted" at the end. Install a SIGTERM handler that raises SystemExit so the finally block runs. Have the dashboard warn when status is not complete.

title: Install trust anchored to unpinned git HEAD; publish job grants contents:write job-wide with checkout-persisted token readable by tag-pinned actions
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: These parts are confirmed. readme.md:53 recommends `pipx install git+https://github.com/0xj4f/aws-enumerator.git` with no @ref, even though v0.2.N tags exist. The package is not on PyPI (pypi.org/pypi/aws-enumerator/json returns 404). `permissions: contents: write` is set at workflow level (docker-publish.yml:12-13), so it covers every step, although only the final tag step (:56-61) needs it. actions/checkout@v4 (:22) persists the GITHUB_TOKEN in .git/config by default, so code in the later major-tag-pinned docker/login-action@v3, setup-buildx-action@v3 and build-push-action@v6 (:37, :43, :46) can read a contents:write token. Because main is unprotected (P3-001), that token could push to main, and pipx users would pick up the change on their next install. A GITHUB_TOKEN push does not trigger a new workflow run, so the image itself would not be rebuilt by that path. The tag-pinning and no-checks parts duplicate F-130 and F-065. The 'third-party actions' framing is overstated: these are the official GitHub and Docker publisher actions. What is new beyond F-130 is the job-wide write scope combined with the persisted token, and the unpinned-HEAD install recommendation.
evidence: docker-publish.yml:12-13 permissions contents: write (workflow level); :22 actions/checkout@v4 with no persist-credentials: false; :37/:43/:46 @v3/@v3/@v6; :56-61 the only step needing write; readme.md:53 pipx install from git URL without @ref; repo default_workflow_permissions is 'read', and the workflow overrides it.
impact: A compromised action tag gets a token that can rewrite main or tags in addition to the image, and every pipx user installs whatever is on main at install time, with no way to pin to a reviewed release.
fix: Split into two jobs: build-and-push with `permissions: contents: read` and `persist-credentials: false`, then a tag job with `contents: write` that `needs:` the first. Pin actions by SHA (F-130). In the README, recommend `pipx install git+https://github.com/0xj4f/aws-enumerator.git@v0.2.N` (or publish to PyPI with trusted publishing) and document how to verify a release.

title: Release path has no human gate: main unprotected, no rulesets, and the 'Development' environment (which holds the Docker Hub secrets) has no protection rules or branch policy
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed with read-only GitHub API calls on 2026-10-12. branches/main returns protected:false with enforcement_level off. rulesets returns []. Environment 'Development' has protection_rules [] and deployment_branch_policy null. DOCKER_USER and DOCKER_PASSWORD are environment-scoped secrets of 'Development', and there are no repo-level secrets, so the environment settings are the only gate on the publishing credentials. The workflow triggers on any push to main (docker-publish.yml:3-5), runs in that environment (:18) and pushes both :<version> and :latest (:50-52). Recent PRs #13 and #14 were opened and merged by the maintainer within about 14 s. F-130 covers missing workflow-level gates (tests, scans, signing, pinning). F-131 explicitly says it could not determine whether the environment has protection rules. This finding settles that question and adds the repository-settings angle (no review or approval gate, and no branch restriction on the environment secrets), so it is kept as a related finding rather than a duplicate. Caveat: for a single-maintainer repo, required PR reviews cannot be self-satisfied. The useful controls are an environment required-reviewer or wait timer, a main-only deployment branch policy, and a ruleset that blocks direct pushes and force pushes, including from GITHUB_TOKEN. Cross-file: complements P3-002.
evidence: gh api repos/0xj4f/aws-enumerator/branches/main -> {"protected":false,"protection":{"enabled":false,"required_status_checks":{"enforcement_level":"off"}}}; gh api .../rulesets -> []; .../environments -> Development {protection_rules: [], deployment_branch_policy: null}; .../environments/Development/secrets -> [DOCKER_PASSWORD, DOCKER_USER]; .../actions/secrets -> []; .../actions/permissions -> allowed_actions 'all', sha_pinning_required false. docker-publish.yml:3-5, :18, :39-40, :50-52.
impact: Any credential or token that can push to main (a stolen maintainer session or PAT, or a GITHUB_TOKEN with contents:write; see P3-002) publishes a new :latest image, with no approval step, that operators run with AWS credentials. Any branch whose workflow names environment Development can read the Docker Hub password. The likelihood is low for a solo project, but the blast radius is every :latest user.
fix: Add a ruleset on main that blocks force pushes and deletion and requires a PR plus a status check once CI exists (F-065). Give the Development environment a deployment branch policy that allows only main or v* tags, plus a required reviewer or wait timer. Optionally set sha_pinning_required and restrict allowed_actions to selected ones. Publish :latest only from signed tags (see F-130).

title: Field guide contains inaccurate technique statements (blind SSRF to IMDS, overwriting a Lambda deployment zip, Principal '*' trust called unauthenticated, 'Buckets with GetSecretValue *')
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: I checked the text at docs/attack_paths.md:63, :244, :261 and :362. (1) IMDSv1 matters for an SSRF that cannot send a PUT or a custom header. A blind SSRF cannot return the credentials, so 'blind SSRF' is wrong. (2) Lambda stores its own copy of the package at CreateFunction/UpdateFunctionCode. Overwriting the S3 object changes nothing until a pipeline or stack redeploys from it, so the line overstates the effect; the next line, about CodePipeline source buckets, is correct. (3) Partially wrong: a Principal '*' trust lets any authenticated principal in any AWS account call sts:AssumeRole, subject to conditions. That is not anonymous access, and 'confused deputy' is the wrong term (it describes service principals without SourceArn/SourceAccount). In the 'external' scenario the intended meaning is close, but the wording is imprecise, and :367 'anyone can assume' has the same problem. (4) 'Buckets with secretsmanager:GetSecretValue *' is incoherent, because buckets do not hold IAM actions; it presumably means principals (DANGER-008). This is distinct from F-067 (graph and dashboard semantics) and F-135 (undocumented IDs).
evidence: attack_paths.md:63 '...useful if you only have a blind SSRF, not RCE'; :244 'Lambda deployment buckets — overwrite the zip, function uses your code'; :261 'Cross-account trust with `*` Principal | Confused deputy / unauthenticated assume | Finding `TRUST-001`'; :362 '5. **Buckets with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue *`**'; :367 'TRUST-001 (anyone can assume)'.
impact: Every finding's reference link points to this playbook. Operators may chase unexploitable leads (blind SSRF, an S3 overwrite with no redeploy) or misdescribe findings in client reports.
fix: Reword :63 as 'useful for a GET-only SSRF that cannot set headers (response must be readable)'. Reword :244 as 'overwrite an artifact that a pipeline or stack later deploys (takes effect on the next UpdateFunctionCode)'. Reword :261 and :367 as 'any principal in any AWS account (attacker needs their own AWS credentials)' and drop 'confused deputy'. Reword :362 as 'Principals with secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on * (DANGER-008)'.

title: No classification or handling guidance for report bundles, although they amount to a pre-computed attack plan
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed: there is no SECURITY.md or data-handling section, the manifest has no classification field (main.py:67-83), and nothing inside the zip warns about its content (main.py:251-256). readme.md:44 says '--zip packages reports for easy transport', lambda_.py:5-6 says env values are dropped 'so the report stays safe to share', and attack_paths.md:13 says 'metadata and policies only'. 'Framed as safe to share' is a stretch: lambda_.py describes a design goal of excluding env values, not a claim about the whole bundle. Still, with no handling guidance the docs understate how sensitive the bundle is: the full IAM graph, privesc findings linked to playbooks, the trust map, logging posture (F-046) and DNS (F-112). Existing coverage: F-123 (file permissions, encryption, operator identity; its fix says 'document secure handling') and F-009/F-054/F-112 (specific sensitive content). The new angle is classifying the dataset as a whole. Report retention on the reviewer's workstation is operator practice, not code. P3-033's data-handling half overlaps this.
evidence: readme.md:44 '`--zip` flag packages reports for easy transport'; lambda_.py:5-6 '...so the report stays safe to share'; docs/attack_paths.md:13 'metadata and policies only'; main.py:67-83 manifest fields (no classification); no SECURITY.md in repo root.
impact: Bundles get emailed, uploaded and kept indefinitely like ordinary scan output. A stolen bundle gives an adversary complete discovery of the account with zero CloudTrail events in the victim account.
fix: Add a 'Handling reports' section: treat bundles as confidential client data, store them encrypted, and set retention. Ship a HANDLING.txt inside each zip and add a "classification" field to the manifest. Remove the 'safe to share' wording from lambda_.py. Pair this with F-123's umask and encryption fix.

title: README Docker recipe mounts the whole ~/.aws read-write into a root container running the floating :latest image
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Both reports describe the same mount, so they are merged. Confirmed. readme.md:83-86 runs `-v ~/.aws:/root/.aws` with no :ro against :latest. The Dockerfile declares VOLUME ["/root/.aws", ...] (:16) and has no USER, so the container runs as root. The container can read every profile, any long-term keys and the sso/cache tokens, which cover every account and permission set assigned to the SSO session. Because the mount is writable, a malicious image could add credential_process to ~/.aws/config, and the host would run it the next time any SDK or CLI used that profile, turning a container compromise into host code execution. Existing coverage: F-132 (root, `-e KEY=$VAL` in argv; its fix already suggests 'a read-only ~/.aws mount with AWS_PROFILE') and F-130 (:latest published unpinned on every push). The new angle is the writable whole-directory mount as a persistence path, plus the reach of the SSO cache. The precondition is an image or dependency compromise (F-130), and AWS documents the same mount pattern for its own aws-cli image, so this stays low. Cross-file: P3-001/P3-002 in new-1 (release path, unpinned trust anchors) raise the likelihood of that precondition.
evidence: readme.md:83-86 `docker run --rm \ -v ~/.aws:/root/.aws \ -v $(pwd)/reports:/app/reports \ 0xj4f/aws-enumerator:latest --region eu-west-2 --zip`; Dockerfile:16 `VOLUME ["/root/.aws", "${WORK_DIR}/reports"]`; Dockerfile has no USER directive; README passes no AWS_PROFILE, so the container uses the default profile while seeing all of them.
impact: A compromised :latest image or dependency would get every credential on the operator's host and could plant persistent host-side code execution through ~/.aws/config.
fix: In the README, use `-v ~/.aws:/home/app/.aws:ro -e AWS_PROFILE=<profile>` once F-132's non-root user is added. Better, export short-lived credentials (`aws configure export-credentials --profile X --format env`) into an --env-file. Pin the image to a version tag or digest instead of :latest, and drop the /root/.aws VOLUME from the Dockerfile.

title: No documented required-permissions set (IAM actions, K8s RBAC), no pre-flight access check, and no SECURITY.md or vulnerability-disclosure channel
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Both reports describe the same missing documentation, so they are merged. Confirmed. The README's 'AWS Credentials' section (readme.md:172-187) only shows how to obtain credentials. There is no IAM policy, managed-policy recommendation or Kubernetes ClusterRole in the README or docs/attack_paths.md. The repo has no SECURITY.md, and GitHub private vulnerability reporting is disabled (read-only `gh api repos/0xj4f/aws-enumerator/private-vulnerability-reporting` -> {"enabled":false}) on a public repo. main.py:205-207 calls only sts:GetCallerIdentity before the 30 collectors run. Missing permissions therefore show up only as silent per-item gaps (F-058/F-059/F-111), swallowed module errors with exit 0 (F-061), or a dashboard crash (F-006); these consequences are already registered, but the missing documentation and pre-flight check are not. P3-033's data-classification point is handled with P3-034. Cross-file: P3-016 in new-1 ('No published permission set; SecurityAudit misses four actions') has the same root cause and should be merged with this at consolidation. P3-007 covers the cluster-wide list-secrets RBAC requirement.
evidence: readme.md:172-187 (credentials only); grep -i 'permission|ReadOnly|SecurityAudit' readme.md -> feature text only (:14, :22-26, :154); repo root has no SECURITY.md (.github holds only workflows/docker-publish.yml); main.py:205-207 is the only pre-collection call; GitHub API: private-vulnerability-reporting enabled=false, visibility public.
impact: Operators cannot provision a least-privilege role. Many will use ReadOnlyAccess, which includes data-plane reads such as s3:GetObject and dynamodb:Scan that the tool never needs, or admin, widening blast radius if the keys leak. Under-privileged runs produce silently incomplete graphs. Researchers have no private channel to report flaws in a tool that runs with production credentials.
fix: Add docs/permissions.md with a JSON policy generated from the collectors' API calls (for example SecurityAudit plus the missing actions) and a minimal ClusterRole: get/list on namespaces, pods, serviceaccounts, roles and bindings, services and ingresses; secrets only if kept. Add a --preflight option (or a start-of-run probe) that makes one cheap read per service and prints or records a coverage table (see F-061 module_status). Add SECURITY.md and enable private vulnerability reporting.

title: Analyzer iterates directories with unsorted os.listdir at 14 sites, making output order and keyed-overwrite winners filesystem-dependent
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed: os.listdir appears unsorted at exactly 14 sites in policy_parser.py (269, 289, 1170, 1696, 1714, 2066, 2078, 2361, 2372, 2593, 2728, 2887, 3072, 3270), and `sorted(os.listdir` matches 0 times. The consequential effects, keyed-overwrite collisions, are already registered as specific bugs: F-013 (policy documents by name) and F-081 (KMS key policies by KeyId). Cross-region mixing comes from the sibling-dir scan in F-025/F-063. Without those collisions, the remaining effect is that findings and edge order can differ between machines for identical inputs. That hurts byte-for-byte comparison and golden tests but not correctness, so this is info. Note that main.py:51 already uses sorted(os.listdir) for the manifest, so the project is inconsistent here.
evidence: grep -n 'os.listdir' app/components/policy_parser.py -> 14 lines listed above; grep -c 'sorted(os.listdir' -> 0; app/main.py:51 `for entry in sorted(os.listdir(base_path))`.
impact: Reports built from the same raw data are not reproducible across filesystems, and which side wins a collision (F-013/F-081) is platform-dependent. There is no correctness impact beyond those registered bugs.
fix: Wrap all 14 sites in sorted(...), or use a helper `_ls(path)` that returns the sorted list. Separately fix the keyed collisions (F-013, F-081) so the outcome does not depend on order.

title: Finding reference links are hard-wired to the GitHub main branch rather than the installed version
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. DOC_BASE = 'https://github.com/0xj4f/aws-enumerator/blob/main/docs/attack_paths.md' (policy_parser.py:3754). Every finding gets reference = DOC_BASE + anchor (:3884-3885), and the dashboard renders it as a link (index.html:2525-2526). docs/ is not packaged: pyproject.toml:38-40 package-data has only regions.json and the dashboard assets. Links inside delivered reports therefore resolve to whatever main says at click time, anchors can disappear when headings change (F-088 already shows a missing ELB anchor), and the links need internet access. This is related to the doc-drift cluster in F-088/F-135 but is a distinct cause (branch pinning). Rated info: it affects the documentation links only, not analysis.
evidence: policy_parser.py:3754 DOC_BASE; :3884-3885 f['reference'] = _doc_reference(...); index.html:2525-2526 href=f.reference; pyproject.toml:38-40 package-data excludes docs/.
impact: Over time, report links point at changed or missing guidance, and they do not work offline or in air-gapped review environments.
fix: Build DOC_BASE from the release tag (for example .../blob/v{VERSION}/docs/attack_paths.md once F-122 gives a real version), or ship docs/attack_paths.md as package data and copy it into the report bundle, linking relatively. Add a test that every _DOC_ANCHORS value exists as a heading.

title: Chronological analyzer groupings ('newsurface', 'extra') are baked into the report file contract and labels already disagree
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. analyze() writes analysis/newsurface_relationships.json and analysis/extra_relationships.json (policy_parser.py:3920-3924), and the dashboard reads them by those names (index.html:1012-1013). The groupings reflect when the analyzers were added, not their domain: newsurface covers ECR/RDS/API Gateway/DynamoDB (:2941-2943, comment :3872) and extra covers Cognito/EBS/ELB/Route53 (:3079-3081, comment :3877). The console line at :3980 says 'Cognito/EBS/ELB relationships' and omits Route53. This is a maintainability observation with no functional defect. It belongs with F-084 (policy_parser structure) and F-088 (label drift).
evidence: policy_parser.py:3920-3924, :3872, :3877, :3980; index.html:1012-1013 readJSON('analysis/newsurface_relationships.json' / 'analysis/extra_relationships.json').
impact: Contributors cannot predict where a service's analysis lives, and reorganising the analyzers by service becomes a report-format change.
fix: When F-084's table-driven refactor happens, emit per-service files (or one relationships.json with a service field) together with a schema_version. Have the dashboard read by schema and keep fallback reads of the old names for one release. Fix the :3980 label now.

title: No deliverable export (CSV/SARIF/Markdown/HTML) of findings or attack paths
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed as a feature gap. A grep of index.html for csv|sarif|export|download|Blob(|createObjectURL finds nothing. The only control is 'Load Report (.zip)' (index.html:596-598). The Python side writes only analysis/*.json (policy_parser.py:3887-3928) and has no CSV, SARIF or Markdown writer. F-141 covers the missing graph or BloodHound export, and F-005 covers non-IAM findings being invisible in the dashboard. Neither covers a findings deliverable (table, SARIF or report), so this is kept as a related, distinct gap. It is not a defect, so it is rated info.
evidence: grep -niE 'csv|sarif|export|download|blob\(|createObjectURL' app/dashboard/index.html -> no matches; index.html:596-598; policy_parser.py:3887-3888 findings.json only.
impact: Consultants and defenders must turn raw JSON into a client or ticket deliverable by hand, which compounds F-005 (resource findings not listed in the UI).
fix: Add `--format csv,sarif,md` to analyze() (SARIF 2.1.0 with ruleId = finding id, plus the fingerprint from the P3-011/P3-013 fix), and an 'Export findings / Export path' button in the dashboard that downloads CSV or Markdown via Blob.

title: Collector entry point named 'enumerate' shadows the Python builtin in all 30 collector modules
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed: `grep -l '^def enumerate('` matches 30 files in app/components/. No collector currently calls the builtin enumerate(): every other `enumerate(` match is a def line. If a contributor writes `for i, x in enumerate(items)` inside a collector, the call resolves to the module's own enumerate(session, path). That raises TypeError or misbehaves, and run_module (app/main.py:89-98) catches every Exception and prints only '<label> module failed', so the whole module's output is lost. This is a latent trap with no current defect, so it is rated info. It is not in the register (F-084 covers only policy_parser maintainability).
evidence: grep -ln '^def enumerate(' app/components/*.py | wc -l -> 30; grep -n 'enumerate(' app/components/*.py excluding def lines -> no matches; app/main.py:96-98 `except Exception as e: print(... module failed ...)`.
impact: No current impact. A future edit could silently drop an entire collector's output, and nothing would catch it because there are no tests (F-065).
fix: Rename the entry point (for example `collect(session, path)` or `run`), keep `enumerate = collect` as a temporary alias, and update main.py. Alternatively, add ruff with rule A001 to CI so that any in-module use of the builtin is flagged.

title: Tool-specific CloudTrail shape fingerprints beyond the UA token (per-SG ENI loop, includeShadowTrails=false, NoSuchEntity bursts, one credential resolution per Session)
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The code facts are confirmed. sg.py:29-33 calls describe_network_interfaces with a group-id filter inside the per-SG loop. cloudtrail.py:10 passes includeShadowTrails=False explicitly. iam.py calls get_login_profile per user, which returns NoSuchEntity for users without a password. app/utils/aws_utils.py:8-9 creates a fresh boto3.Session for each get_boto3_session call (main.py:205, :221, :234), and waf.py:32 builds another Session for CLOUDFRONT scope. botocore's default credential cache is per Session, so assume-role and SSO profiles resolve credentials once per Session: 2 in single-region mode (main plus the WAF rebuild), and N+3 in --all (main, global, global WAF rebuild, one per region), which reveals the region count. Several pieces are already registered for other reasons: the ENI-per-SG and NoSuchEntity volume in F-109, includeShadowTrails correctness in F-045, and the UA token in F-125. The new part is treating their combination as a detection signature. I did not verify how CloudTrail records these requestParameters, and the reporter flagged the same gap. Info: useful for detection engineering and red-team OPSEC notes, not a defect. Cross-file: P3-026 (self-identification).
evidence: sg.py:29-33; cloudtrail.py:10 describe_trails(includeShadowTrails=False); iam.py get_login_profile per user (F-109 evidence); aws_utils.py get_boto3_session -> boto3.Session(region_name=region); main.py:205, :221, :234; waf.py:32 session.__class__(profile_name=..., region_name='us-east-1').
impact: Defenders can fingerprint the tool from CloudTrail shape alone. Red teams get more distinctive telemetry than the README implies, including one AssumeRole or GetRoleCredentials event per region in --all.
fix: Document the fingerprint in the README (for defenders and as an OPSEC note). Create one Session and derive regional clients with session.client(svc, region_name=r) so credentials resolve once. Replace per-SG ENI calls with one paginated DescribeNetworkInterfaces (F-109). Drop includeShadowTrails=False (F-045). Optionally set AWS_SDK_UA_APP_ID for deliberate self-identification (P3-026).

title: Report manifest has no per-file digests and no signature, so a stored report cannot be shown to be unmodified
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The facts are correct. generate_manifest records only relative file names and counts (main.py:52-65). Its fields (:67-83) carry no digest, commit or signature. The zip is a plain shutil.make_archive (:252-255, :278-281), and the dashboard verifies nothing. The missing build SHA is already F-122, whose fix writes git_sha into the manifest. What is new is per-file hashes and signing, and that value is limited. Hashes stored inside the same zip give no tamper evidence, because whoever edits a file can also edit the manifest. Only an out-of-band digest or a detached signature with a trust anchor would help, and a browser page has no key distribution to check one against. The issue also says missing integrity 'enables' the F-097 injection, but that injection is caused by missing escaping (F-008/F-097), not missing signatures. Rated info: it matters only when reports are used as evidence.
evidence: main.py:52-65 builds modules[].files from os.walk with no hashing; main.py:67-83 manifest keys are tool, version, author, run_metadata and modules_executed; main.py:252-255/278-281 shutil.make_archive; index.html:917-937 loads any zip.
impact: Nobody can later prove that an archived report is unmodified tool output, which weakens its use as incident or remediation evidence. The tool's own security is not affected.
fix: Add a sha256 per file to the manifest (cheap corruption detection), and print the zip's SHA-256 at the end of the run so operators can record it out of band. Optionally add --sign to produce a detached minisign/cosign/gpg signature. Fix the escaping in F-008/F-097 regardless.

title: No logging framework: 134 print() calls with hard-coded ANSI colours and no levels, quiet mode, NO_COLOR or TTY detection
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed: `grep -rn 'print(' app --include='*.py' | wc -l` = 134. No module imports logging. ANSI escapes are hard-coded in every message (for example main.py:98 and aws_utils.py:32). There is no isatty, NO_COLOR, --quiet or --json handling. The issue's second half, silent per-item failures, is already in the register: F-059 (secretsmanager.py:76-77, the line cited here), F-058 (S3 sub-calls, s3.py:69-137), F-111 (IAM inline policies), F-102 and F-061 (module failures only printed, exit 0). The new part is the missing logging framework and colour codes in captured logs. That is an operability polish item: coloured console output is normal for an interactive offensive CLI, and the machine-readable run status belongs in the manifest (F-061's fix).
evidence: print( count 134 across app/*.py; grep 'import logging' under app/ -> no matches; grep NO_COLOR|isatty|quiet -> none; main.py:98 `print(f"    \033[1;31m[-]\033[0m {label} module failed: {e}")`; secretsmanager.py:76-77 `except ClientError: pass`.
impact: Output captured by CI, CloudWatch or Kubernetes contains escape codes and has no levels to filter on. Coverage loss from per-item errors is invisible (tracked in F-058/F-059/F-111).
fix: Add a module logger that uses a colour formatter only when stderr.isatty() and NO_COLOR is unset. Log per-item ClientError codes at debug or warning level, and add --quiet/--verbose. Keep the per-module status from F-061 in the manifest as the machine-readable record.

title: No self-identifying user-agent token or run ID, so SOCs cannot tie API traffic to an authorised run
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: The facts are confirmed. grep for user_agent, UA_APP, user_agent_extra and app_id in app/ finds nothing, and the manifest has no run ID (main.py:67-83). An offline botocore 1.37.34 check (fake credentials, request stopped in a before-send hook) shows no app/ token in the User-Agent by default. With AWS_SDK_UA_APP_ID=aws-enumerator-0.2.0, it contains app/aws-enumerator-0.2.0. F-125's fix already says to 'expose user_agent_extra / AWS_SDK_UA_APP_ID for UA control', but frames it as OPSEC. This issue adds blue-team deconfliction and a run ID. Operators can already set AWS_SDK_UA_APP_ID themselves, because boto3 honours it. A default identifying token works against red-team stealth, so it should be a documented option, not forced. Cross-file: P3-013 in new-1 (findings.json carries no run context) overlaps on the run ID.
evidence: Repro (scratchpad agents/verify-new-2/ua.py): `None -> []`, `aws-enumerator-0.2.0 -> ['app/aws-enumerator-0.2.0']`; main.py:202-203 sets only retry env vars; main.py:67-83 manifest has no run_id.
impact: In CloudTrail and Kubernetes audit logs, an authorised assessment looks like any other boto3 client, which slows SOC triage and deconfliction during engagements. This is not a security control.
fix: Generate a uuid4 run_id at start and write it to the manifest. Set Config(user_agent_appid=f'aws-enumerator/{VERSION}/{run_id}') unless --no-ua-tag is given. Document this, and role-session naming, for SOC deconfliction.

title: Report date folder and manifest timestamps use naive local time with no UTC offset
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. date_today (main.py:209), start_time (:211), end_time (:49) and the banner date (:41) all come from naive datetime.now(). The manifest's timestamp_start and timestamp_end are isoformat strings with no offset. In the repro, timestamp_start was '2026-10-12T11:48:45.476339'. The folder date therefore depends on the host's timezone (a UTC container versus a local laptop), and timestamps from different hosts cannot be compared reliably. The same-day collision itself is F-063's root cause; this only changes which runs collide.
evidence: main.py:209 `date_today = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d")`; main.py:78-79 `start_time.isoformat()`/`end_time.isoformat()`; repro_main.py output `timestamp_start: 2026-10-12T11:48:45.476339` (no offset).
impact: Freshness, retention and merge behaviour vary with host timezone, and cross-host timelines can be misread.
fix: Use datetime.now(timezone.utc) for the start and end times and for the folder date, or at least isoformat() on an aware value, and record the timezone in the manifest.

title: No authorised-use / rules-of-engagement statement for a dual-use offensive tool
review_trail: single verifier (perspective-raised, below medium; no second opinion required)
explanation: Confirmed. readme.md:1-8, docs/attack_paths.md and the CLI banner (main.py:30-44) contain no authorised-use or rules-of-engagement statement. grep for authori, legal and written permission finds only API Gateway authorizer text and engagement-reporting advice (attack_paths.md:421). LICENSE is MIT, which has a warranty disclaimer only. The legal effect the report describes is speculative, so this is documentation hygiene that dual-use tools commonly include. The related technical control is F-062 (no K8s opt-out).
evidence: readme.md:3-7 framing ('Built for offensive security and assumed breach scenarios'); main.py:32-43 banner; grep -in 'authori|legal|written|consent' readme.md docs/attack_paths.md -> only APIGW authorizer rows; LICENSE line 1 'MIT License'.
impact: Operators get no reminder to obtain written authorisation and confirm scope (including the EKS/K8s plane) before a run that enumerates cluster secrets automatically.
fix: Add a short 'Authorized use only' section to the README and attack_paths.md covering written authorisation, scope including EKS/K8s, and data handling, and add one line to the banner.
